Lumbar disk degeneration

At three months, 785 nm low-level laser and 1064 nm high-intensity laser did not outperform placebo for pain, disability, or mobility. An uncontrolled intradiscal laser series reported a 14% increase in disc MRI signal intensity, without a patient control group.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

At three months, 785 nm low-level laser and 1064 nm high-intensity laser did not outperform placebo for pain, disability, or mobility. An uncontrolled intradiscal laser series reported a 14% increase in disc MRI signal intensity, without a patient control group.

Summary of the Evidence

Two unique human publications address lumbar disc degeneration. One is a 68-person controlled study of transcutaneous laser and the other a 28-person single-arm intradiscal procedure. They involve distinct participants and different routes of delivery; the latter is not conventional non-invasive PBM. No reviews or independent replications were counted as additional trials.

Human and clinical evidence

Taradaj and colleagues compared 785 nm low-level laser therapy and 1064 nm high-intensity laser therapy with placebo. Pain, disability, and mobility improved over time in the study groups, but neither active laser arm showed a significant between-group advantage on those outcomes at three months. The article describes a controlled study, not a randomized trial. Borshchenko and colleagues treated 28 patients with transforaminal intradiscal 1560 nm erbium-fiber laser. They reported a 14% increase in irradiated-disc MRI signal intensity and follow-up observations extending to five years, but there was no untreated patient comparator (Taradaj et al. 2018 Borshchenko et al. 2022).

Animal evidence

No animal study specific to lumbar disc degeneration was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The controlled study used 785 nm near-infrared low-level laser and 1064 nm near-infrared high-intensity laser. The separate intradiscal study used a 1560 nm near-infrared fiber laser placed inside the disc. These wavelengths, power levels, routes, and treatment targets are not interchangeable. The database does not provide a complete dose schedule for every arm, so missing settings are not inferred.

Interpretation

The controlled transcutaneous evidence does not show an advantage over placebo on the principal clinical outcomes. The MRI change after invasive treatment is an imaging observation without a control group and does not establish symptom relief or disease modification.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A 68-person placebo-controlled study found no significant between-group advantage for low-level or high-intensity laser on its main clinical outcomes at three months. A separate 28-person uncontrolled intradiscal study reported an MRI signal change, but it used an invasive procedure and had no untreated control. Longer independent trials should separate these interventions and measure patient-important outcomes.
